title: Who Poisoned Mehmed the Conqueror?
titles: The Sultan's Doctor Offered to Kill Him
How Did Fatih Sultan Mehmed Really Die?
description: In May 1481, Mehmed the Conqueror, the sultan who took Constantinople at 21, died in a tent near Gebze after two days of stomach pain, and his death was hidden from his own army. Vix opens the file: his rise, the conquest of 1453, Venice's Council of Ten and its plots, the doctor who once offered to kill him, the cover-up, and the four suspects. Poison is possible. Is it proven?

summary_short.hook: The sultan's doctor offered to kill him
summary_short.say: In 1471, the personal doctor of Mehmed the Conqueror made Venice an offer. He would kill the sultan. For money, and Venetian citizenship. Venice took it seriously. Then nothing happened. For ten years, that doctor stayed at the sultan's side. In May 1481, Mehmed fell sick on campaign near Gebze. His chief doctor failed. So they called the old one back. The same man. His medicine did nothing. Mehmed died at forty-nine. His death was hidden from the army. Within days, the grand vizier was killed. And so, by several accounts, was the doctor. Poison? Possible. Proven? Never. The full story is on the channel.

Second reign from February 1451

scenes.say: May the third, 1481. A field near Gebze, one day's ride from Istanbul. Inside a guarded tent, the most powerful man in the Islamic world is dying... and nobody will say why.

scenes.say: Two days of agony. Pain in his stomach that no doctor could stop. Then silence. And within hours, the men around him start lying to an entire army.
I'm Vix. Every case has a loose thread. And this one has been hanging loose for five hundred and forty-five years.
The victim? Mehmed the Second. The man the world calls Fatih... the Conqueror. The man who took Constantinople at twenty-one.

scenes.say: The suspects? A secret council in Venice. His own doctor. A rival sultan in Cairo. And maybe... his own son.
To understand who wanted him dead, we have to understand who he was. So let's open the file. From the very first page.
Edirne, 1432. This was the Ottoman capital then, not Istanbul. On March the thirtieth, Sultan Murad the Second gets a new son. Mehmed.
Here's the first detail people miss. He wasn't supposed to be sultan. He was the third son. His mother, Hüma Hatun, was a palace slave. Nobody bet on this boy.

visuals.caption: Ruins of the old palace at Edirne

scenes.say: Then his older brothers die, one after another. And at eleven, Mehmed is sent to govern the city of Amasya, with tutors watching every move he makes.

visuals.caption: Amasya, where he governed as a boy

scenes.say: Now watch what happens in 1444. His father does something no one expects. He gives up the throne. Mehmed is twelve years old... and he is sultan.

search: Mehmed II smelling a rose miniature Topkapi
Nakkas Sinan Bey Mehmed II rose
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, Ottoman miniature, 15th century

scenes.say: It lasts about two years. A crusader army marches in. The viziers panic. Murad comes back, wins at Varna in November 1444, and soon takes the throne back.

There's a famous line from this moment. Later chronicles say young Mehmed wrote to his father: if you are the sultan, come and lead your armies. If I am the sultan, I order you to come and lead my armies. A boy giving his father an order.

search: Mehmed II smelling a rose miniature Topkapi
Nakkas Sinan Bey Mehmed II rose
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, Ottoman miniature, 15th century

scenes.say: Historians still argue about who pushed for that. One strong suspect is the grand vizier, Çandarlı Halil Pasha. Remember that name. The boy certainly did.
So Mehmed is sent away to Manisa. Still called sultan. But with no real power. A teenager who has tasted the throne... and had it taken from him.

Gentile Bellini portrait of Mehmed II 1480 National Gallery
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, by Gentile Bellini, 1480

scenes.say: In 1451, Murad dies. And this time, nobody can stop him. Mehmed is about nineteen. And he already knows exactly what he wants.
Constantinople. A thousand years of Roman emperors. Walls that had stopped army after army. Everyone told him it couldn't be done.
Look at that. Not one wall. Two walls, and a moat in front. Three lines of defense. That's what a twenty-one-year-old decided to break.

visuals.quote: how the walls of Constantinople worked

scenes.say: So first, he builds a fortress. Right on the Bosphorus, the narrowest point. In 1452, in a matter of months. Rumelihisarı.
Look at those towers. Built in about four months. And the Venetians and Byzantines watched every stone go up.
Look at where it stands. Across the water is an older Ottoman fort. Together, they close the strait. Nothing reaches the city by sea without his permission.
Then he hires a cannon-maker named Orban. A Hungarian, some say. Orban had offered his guns to the Byzantines first. They couldn't pay him. Mehmed could.

visuals.caption: The Great Turkish Bombard, cast in 1464 for Mehmed II

scenes.say: This is a real Ottoman bombard from his reign. Cast in 1464, now in England. Nearly seventeen tons of bronze. Imagine the ones that hit those walls.

visuals.caption: The Great Turkish Bombard, Royal Armouries

scenes.say: Look at the size of that mouth. Stone balls, hundreds of kilos each. Now picture dozens of guns like this, firing for weeks.

visuals.search: Great Turkish Bombard Royal Armouries Fort Nelson

scenes.say: April 1453. The siege begins. A huge army, tens of thousands strong. Inside, Emperor Constantine the Eleventh has only a few thousand defenders.
How big? Estimates run from eighty thousand to two hundred thousand men. More than seventy big guns. And a fleet of hundreds of ships. Against walls that had never once been broken by force.

search: Siege of Constantinople Ottoman artillery painting
visuals.caption: Ottoman guns at the siege

scenes.say: For weeks, the guns pound the walls. Every night, the defenders patch the holes with wood, earth and barrels. Every morning, the guns knock them down again.

visuals.caption: Damaged towers of the land walls

scenes.say: See that gap? That's where it ends. Not with a trick. With weeks of iron and stone hitting the same place.

visuals.search: Siege of Constantinople 1453 documentary walls cannon

scenes.say: And the harbor, the Golden Horn, is sealed with a giant chain. His ships can't get in. So what does a twenty-one-year-old do?

search: Golden Horn chain Istanbul Military Museum
visuals.caption: Links of the Golden Horn chain

scenes.say: Links said to be from that chain are still kept in Istanbul today. Forged iron, made to stop an entire fleet.

visuals.search: Golden Horn chain Istanbul Military Museum

scenes.say: April twenty-second. He drags his ships over land. Over a hill, on greased wooden tracks, and down into the harbor behind the chain.

search: Mehmed II ships over land Golden Horn
visuals.caption: The fleet carried over land, 1453

scenes.say: Fifty-seven days of siege. Then, on May the twenty-ninth, 1453, the walls break. Constantine dies fighting. The Roman Empire... ends.

scenes.say: The last attack comes before dawn. Wave after wave. First irregular troops, then regular soldiers. And finally, the sultan's own elite. The Janissaries.

search: Fall of Constantinople final assault painting
visuals.caption: The final assault, 1453

scenes.say: He rides into Hagia Sophia. The greatest church in Christendom. And it becomes a mosque. He is twenty-one years old.
Look up at that dome. Nine hundred years old when he walked in. And he chose not to tear it down. He made it his.
Remember Çandarlı Halil, the vizier from the first page? Within weeks of the conquest, he's arrested. And executed. The boy remembered.
And he gives himself a new title. Kayser-i Rum. Caesar of Rome. In his mind, he didn't destroy the Roman Empire. He inherited it.

search: Mehmed II medal Costanzo da Ferrara
visuals.caption: Medal of Mehmed II, about 1481
A Byzantine emperor, Hagia Sophia mosaic

scenes.say: From here, the file gets thick. Very thick. Because Mehmed doesn't stop. Almost every year, there's a new campaign.
Serbia falls. The Morea, in Greece, falls. In 1461, the empire of Trebizond on the Black Sea surrenders. The last Greek state.
But he loses too. At Belgrade, in 1456, his attack fails and he's wounded himself. Mehmed is not invincible. He just never quits.
In 1462, he crosses the Danube to punish a prince of Wallachia. You know him by another name. Vlad the Impaler.
Vlad attacks his camp at night. The sultan survives. He marches on, takes Vlad's capital, and puts Vlad's own brother, Radu, on the throne.

search: The Battle with Torches Theodor Aman
visuals.caption: The Night Attack, by Theodor Aman

scenes.say: Bosnia, 1463. And that same year, a war begins that will last sixteen years. Against the richest sea power in the world. Venice.

search: Venice Grand Canal old painting Canaletto
visuals.caption: Venice

scenes.say: In the east, in 1473, he crushes the Turkmen ruler Uzun Hasan at Otlukbeli. Now his empire reaches from the Danube deep into Anatolia.
But here's the part people forget. This conqueror reads Greek and Persian books. He collects Italian art. He builds Topkapı Palace, and a huge mosque complex with schools around it.

visuals.caption: The Tiled Kiosk, built for Mehmed II

scenes.say: This was the gate to his world. Behind it, the doctors, the viziers, the secrets. Remember this place.
And in 1479, he asks Venice, his old enemy, to send him their best painter. They send Gentile Bellini. That's the portrait you've been looking at.

search: Gentile Bellini portrait of Mehmed II 1480 National Gallery
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, by Gentile Bellini, 1480

scenes.say: Look at his eyes in that painting. Tired. Thin face. A man who doesn't have long. And the painter was sent by Venice.

visuals.search: Gentile Bellini portrait Mehmed II National Gallery

scenes.say: And one more thing from his reign. Remember this one, because it comes back at the end. Mehmed writes a law about his own family.
It says, roughly: whichever of my sons takes the throne may put his brothers to death, for the order of the world. Brother against brother... written into law.
Look closely at that face. Thin. Tired. Painted around 1480. A year later, he's dead. Was that painter just a painter? Hold that thought.

search: Gentile Bellini portrait of Mehmed II 1480 National Gallery
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, by Gentile Bellini, 1480

scenes.say: To find our first suspect, we go to Venice. Not to the Doge. To a room upstairs in his palace. The room of the Council of Ten.

search: Hall of the Council of Ten Doge's Palace
visuals.caption: Hall of the Council of Ten

scenes.say: This is the room. Ten seats. Ten men. Some of the decisions taken here had one goal: a dead sultan.

visuals.search: Doge's Palace Venice Council of Ten hall tour

scenes.say: Ten nobles, elected every year. Venice's secret service. Spies, informers, sealed files. And when they wanted someone gone quietly, their favorite tool was poison.

visuals.caption: A 'lion's mouth', for secret denunciations, Venice

search: dropper bottle liquid close up dark

scenes.say: Now, this isn't a rumor. The Council's own records were studied by historians, especially Franz Babinger. They show plot after plot to kill the sultan.
And Mehmed wasn't blind. He had spies too. In 1470, a Venetian go-between named David Mavrogonato was killed in Istanbul on his fourth trip, likely by Ottoman intelligence.

visuals.caption: Galata, the Italian quarter of Istanbul

scenes.say: One account counts about a dozen attempts between 1456 and 1479. Most never got past planning. But some got very close.
Around 1464, a Spaniard named Manuel Cerda offers to do it. The Ten promise him ten thousand ducats. It fails.
In 1475, there's a plan to send a doctor called Valchus into Istanbul. He reportedly gets inside the palace. And again... the sultan lives.
But the most dangerous offer in the whole file doesn't come from a stranger. It comes from inside the sultan's own circle. From his doctor.
His name was Jacopo. Born in Gaeta, Italy, around 1425. A Jewish doctor who came to the Ottoman court when Mehmed's father still ruled.
He becomes the sultan's personal physician. Converts to Islam. Takes the name Yakub. And rises all the way to the rank of pasha.
Think about what that means. For about thirty years, this man is closer to Mehmed's body than anyone. He knows every pain. Every medicine. Every cup.

search: tea cup steam dark close up

scenes.say: And in 1471, according to the Venetian records, Maestro Jacopo makes the Ten an offer. He'll kill the sultan.

His price? Money up front, freedom from taxes, Venetian citizenship for his family. And one later account says Venice agreed to ten thousand gold pieces in advance, and twenty-five thousand more if the sultan died in early 1472.

visuals.label: reported total, if the sultan died

scenes.say: The records show the Ten took him seriously. But 1472 comes and goes. The sultan is alive. Jacopo stays at his side. For nine more years.

scenes.say: So here's the question. Was it a scam to squeeze money out of Venice? Or a man waiting for the right moment? Keep that question open.
1479. Venice finally signs a peace treaty. Bellini comes to paint. And Mehmed turns his armies further west than ever before.

search: Gentile Bellini portrait of Mehmed II 1480 National Gallery
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, by Gentile Bellini, 1480
Venice, 1500 view by Jacopo de' Barbari

scenes.say: In 1480, his fleet attacks Rhodes, and fails. But another force lands in Italy itself and takes the city of Otranto. Rome is in a panic.

search: Palace of the Grand Master Rhodes
visuals.caption: Rhodes

scenes.say: This is Otranto. An Ottoman army, on Italian soil, in 1480. You can understand why Rome was terrified.
Spring, 1481. A huge army gathers. And Mehmed tells nobody where it's going. Italy? Rhodes? The Mamluks in Egypt? Historians still argue.
But one detail matters more than the destination. He was already sick when he left Istanbul. He suffered from gout, like many sultans. Swollen, painful joints.

visuals.caption: Üsküdar, where the army crossed to Asia

search: old man hand pain close up dark

scenes.say: He crosses to the Asian side. He's in so much pain, one chronicle says, that he travels by carriage. Not on horseback. The Conqueror, in a cart.
He reaches a meadow near Gebze. Hünkâr Çayırı. The sultan's meadow. And here, it gets much worse.
His chief physician now is a Persian, Hamidüddin al-Lari. Lari treats him. Nothing works. The pain is now in his stomach. Terrible pain.
So they call the old doctor back. Yakub Pasha. The same Jacopo from the Venetian file.
And here's a strange detail. Yakub doesn't want to step in. He disapproves of what Lari gave the sultan. The other doctors are lost. Finally, he gives his own syrup for the pain.

search: pouring syrup bottle dark close up

scenes.say: It does nothing. On May the third, 1481, between the afternoon and evening prayers, Mehmed the Conqueror dies. He is forty-nine.

search: Gentile Bellini portrait of Mehmed II 1480 National Gallery
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, by Gentile Bellini, 1480

scenes.say: Two doctors. One who'd once offered to kill him for money. One who failed to save him. Both standing in that tent.
What happens next tells us something. The grand vizier, Karamani Mehmed Pasha, hides the death. From the army. From everyone.
The body is sent back to Istanbul in secret. The soldiers are told the sultan has gone to the city... to visit a bathhouse.
One servant later remembered that for three days and nights, no candle was lit beside the sultan's body. Think about that. The Conqueror, alone in the dark.
Why hide it? Because Mehmed had two sons. Bayezid, the elder, in Amasya. And Cem, the younger, in Konya. And the grand vizier wanted Cem.
Konya is closer. He sends riders racing to Cem. Whoever reaches Istanbul first... gets the empire.
And remember Mehmed's law. Whoever wins may kill the loser. So this isn't a race for a crown. It's a race to stay alive.
But the Janissaries, the sultan's elite soldiers, find out. They suspect the vizier is backing Cem. And they explode.
They kill Karamani Mehmed Pasha. They loot the houses of the rich. And according to several accounts, they also kill Yakub Pasha. The doctor.
Notice something? Within days, the two men who knew the most about that tent can never answer a single question.
Bayezid wins the race. He becomes Sultan Bayezid the Second. Cem fights him, loses, and flees to Egypt, then ends his life as a prisoner in Europe.

visuals.caption: Prince Cem, in a fresco by Pinturicchio

scenes.say: And in Venice? A messenger arrives on May the nineteenth. His news, as the story goes: the Great Eagle is dead.
Meanwhile in Italy, the army at Otranto is cut off. No reinforcements come. The city is retaken. Italy is spared.
So. Five centuries later, let's do what nobody could do in 1481. Let's look at the suspects. One by one.
Suspect one. Venice, through Yakub Pasha. Motive: sixteen years of war. Means: the doctor at his bedside. And a written offer to kill him, sitting in Venice's own archive.

search: old letter wax seal close up

scenes.say: But the offer was ten years old. Venice was at peace by 1481. And Yakub had nine years of chances before that. Why wait until then?
Suspect two. His own son, Bayezid, using the Persian doctor Lari. Motive: the grand vizier wanted Cem on the throne. And under his father's own law, if Cem took the throne, Bayezid would likely die.
And Lari? He died in Edirne in 1485. Rumor said Bayezid forced him to take too much opium. A doctor who knew too much? Or just gossip? We can't prove either.
Suspect three. Qaitbay, the Mamluk sultan of Egypt. Some say that's where this last army was really heading. And there are claims the Mamluks had tried to kill Mehmed before.
And suspect four... nobody. A forty-nine-year-old man with gout, already sick, after thirty years of war. For a long time, that was the accepted answer.

scenes.say: So why do historians still say poison? In the twentieth century, Franz Babinger pointed to two clues. A Venetian document. And a poem in the chronicle of Aşıkpaşazade.

search: Mehmed the Conqueror and His Time Babinger
visuals.caption: Franz Babinger

scenes.say: Some read that poem as a hint of a suspicious medicine. Others read it as an angry complaint about bad treatment. Same words. Two meanings.

search: old book page close up candle

scenes.say: Here's what we actually have. A sudden stomach illness. Two failed doctors. A death hidden for days. A vizier and a doctor killed within hours. And an enemy who'd paid for this exact outcome.
What we don't have is a body we can test, a confession, or a single witness who says I saw it happen. So my verdict? Case open. Poison is possible. It is not proven.
Mehmed was buried in the mosque he built, in the city he took. You can still visit his tomb in Istanbul's Fatih district today.

search: Tomb of Mehmed the Conqueror Fatih Mosque
visuals.caption: The tomb of Mehmed II, Istanbul

scenes.say: There he is. The Conqueror. And whatever happened in that tent, the answer is still in there with him.
Three lessons from this file. One: the most dangerous man is rarely the stranger at the gate. It's the one already in the room.
Two: when the powerful die, the first thing that happens is a fight over the story. Who knew, who hid it, who talked.
And three: history doesn't always close its cases. Sometimes the honest answer is: we don't know. Yet.

search: Gentile Bellini portrait of Mehmed II 1480 National Gallery
visuals.caption: Mehmed II, by Gentile Bellini, 1480

scenes.say: So now it's your call. Venice, the son, Egypt... or just a sick man's body giving out? Tell me in the comments. Case closed. For now. I'm Vix.
